prize_parts.citation: for developing methods to estimate demand and competition in differentiated-product markets, which transformed empirical industrial organisation and the analysis of mergers, market power and welfare

statement.case_for: B001 remains my first choice after reading the openings. The random-coefficients demand framework with endogenous prices (BLP, 1995) answers a concrete measurement problem: how to recover substitution patterns and market power from market-level data. The answer is now standard in academic work, in antitrust and merger review, and in applications well outside industrial organisation, such as trade, environmental and health economics. Pakes's dynamic-industry and production-function work (Ericson-Pakes, Olley-Pakes) is a closely related strand that shows the contribution is a programme and not a single paper. The core papers date from the mid-1990s, so about three decades of replication, refinement and regulatory use have tested the contribution. Attribution is also unusually clean. The demand-estimation core is a named trio, and the three-person limit fits it without arbitrary exclusions. I apply the same criteria as for every candidate: originality, durability, breadth of use and clarity of credit. On these B001 does at least as well as any other shortlisted entry. I rank it above my own field's candidate (B009), which I treat strictly under the same standard.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that B001 is mainly a methodological toolkit. Some members may weigh a toolkit below a substantive discovery about the economy. BLP implementations are known to be sensitive to numerical choices and weak identification, and structural results can depend on functional-form assumptions. The cap also makes the credit boundary debatable, since Bresnahan, Reiss, Benkard and Levin all have claims to the wider empirical-IO programme. Finally, the entry pools several strands (demand, production functions, dynamic games), so what exactly is being recognised is a question the citation has to settle.

responses.point: Krusell ranks B001 first but names Bresnahan instead of Levinsohn as the third laureate. He sees Pakes as central across demand, production-function and dynamic-game methods, and Bresnahan as the founder of the new empirical IO. He also says reasonable people could swap the two.
responses.response: I take the swap seriously, and Bresnahan's early work on differentiated-product demand and his role in the new empirical IO programme are real. I still keep Levinsohn. The prize is best tied to the specific, widely used estimator, and that is the BLP trio. Berry's inversion and the joint 1995 paper are where the method is defined. Bresnahan's contribution is more a research agenda that made BLP possible, and its credit is less concentrated in one identifiable result. If the Committee prefers a broader citation on the empirical-IO programme, I would reopen the question, but I would not drop Pakes or Berry in either case.

responses.point: Fredriksson ranks B002 first and B001 second. He also names Bresnahan in the third B001 slot and notes that the cap splits the BLP trio and leaves the credit assignment imperfect.
responses.response: On B001 we agree on Pakes and Berry and differ on the third name. The split of the BLP trio is the reason I would not split it. Excluding a co-author of the central paper is a harder attribution problem than leaving out an adjacent pioneer. On B002 I find the Kiyotaki-Moore mechanism compelling and I list it among my alternatives. I would still not add Gertler, as you do. The accelerator strand is tied to Bernanke's 2022 recognition, which blurs credit and overlap. I read that as a reason for the two-person framing, not a reason to rank B002 above B001.

responses.point: Hjalmarsson ranks B013 first and B001 third. She says committees differ on how to weigh a toolkit against a discovery. She also treats Bresnahan as a possible replacement for Levinsohn and values a combined explanatory framework plus new empirical designs.
responses.response: I agree that the toolkit-versus-discovery weighting is the main open question for B001. My answer is that the discovery here is a measurement capability that changed what can be known about competition and welfare. The tests are whether it altered practice and whether the results held up, and both are met. I respect your case for B013, and its credible designs and its framework are real strengths. For me it falls behind because the China-shock results are still debated in magnitude and persistence, and attribution is split across the technology and trade strands, with Dorn's exclusion. It would be a strong candidate in a later year, but I do not think that debate makes it more mature than B001.

responses.point: Hassler ranks B001 first with the BLP trio and notes that structural estimation has not been recognised by the prize as a tradition. He also ranks B049 second, while recognising that attribution there is crowded and that the framework's performance in the 2021-23 inflation is debated.
responses.response: I agree that the structural-estimation tradition is unrecognised, and that supports timing. I would qualify one point. The fact that a field has not yet been recognised is not evidence of merit, so the case has to rest on the work itself, as you argue. On B049 I share your concern about the three-name cap. The credit is spread over Calvo, Taylor, Woodford, Gali, Christiano, Eichenbaum, Gertler and Smets, so any trio leaves out major contributors. That is the main reason I rank it last and leave it out of my alternatives.

uncertainties: Whether the Committee prefers the narrower BLP trio or a broader empirical-IO citation that would bring in Bresnahan and possibly Reiss, Benkard or Levin.
How much weight a methods-and-tools contribution carries against a substantive discovery, and whether the dynamic-industry strand needs separate credit.
How far BLP results depend on numerical choices and identification assumptions in applied work. I rely on background knowledge and have not independently verified citation or adoption counts.

Whether B009 or B002 should take precedence if B001 is not chosen. My alternatives are a judgement call between overlapping adjacent prizes: the 2024 institutions prize for B009 and the 2022 banking-crisis prize for B002.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile. The profile lists no tie to the B001 candidates or to the B002 candidates. B009 (Persson, Tabellini, Besley) is close to my research field, but the profile names no collaboration with them. My long-time collaborators and V-Dem colleagues are not credited on any shortlisted entry. I gave the 2024 presentation speech on institutions and prosperity, but a speech delivered for the Academy does not establish a preference, and I do not treat it as a conflict.
